title: Passing messages
objectives: Explain one message-passing step as a random-walk step on the graph.

screens.title: Where does the value go?
screens.prose: Venue D holds the value 1 and the others hold 0. One step replaces every venue's value by the mean of its neighbours' values, $\mathbf x \to \mathbf D^{-1}\mathbf A\mathbf x$. Predict, then slide.
screens.question: After one step, which venues hold a value above 0?

options.text: A and D: D keeps half of its 1
options.why: You kept part of D's own value. Without a self-loop D's new value is its neighbour A's old value, 0.
You spread the value over every venue at once. One step moves it only to D's neighbours.

options.text: B and C, the venues far from D
options.why: B and C are two links from D. One step reaches only D's neighbour A.

hints.text: A venue's new value is the mean of its neighbours' old values.
Only A has D as a neighbour; A averages B, C and D: $(0 + 0 + 1)/3$.

feedback.correct: A only: it averages B, C and D, so it holds $\tfrac13$, and D now holds A's old 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out each venue's mean of its neighbours.

explain.text: Each venue takes the mean of its neighbours' values. Only A is next to D, so after one step A holds $\tfrac13$ and the rest hold 0.

screens.title: Many steps
screens.prose: Slide through more steps. Watch whether the four values stop changing.
screens.question: What value does every venue settle on? Give 3 decimal places.

hints.text: Slide to 40 steps and read any venue.
Compare it with D's share of the walk in `markov` l14, $\deg(D)/8$.

feedback.correct: $0.125 = \tfrac18$ at every venue, D's long-run share of the walk.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Slide to 40 steps and read the values.

byKey.even: You split the 1 evenly over four venues. The values settle at $\tfrac18$, not $\tfrac14$.
byKey.zero: The value does not leak away: each step averages, so the values stay between the smallest and largest start.

explain.text: The values settle at $\tfrac18 = 0.125$ everywhere. That is $\pi_D = \deg(D)/8$, D's share of the walk's time in `markov` l14.

screens.title: One step by hand
screens.prose: Name it: a **message-passing step**. Every node collects its neighbours' values and combines them, here by a mean. With the walk's step matrix $\mathbf P = \mathbf D^{-1}\mathbf A$, $(\mathbf P\mathbf x)_i$ is the expected value of $\mathbf x$ where the walker lands next, starting from $i$.
screens.question: Venues hold A 2, B 0, C 4 and D 6. What does B hold after one step?

hints.text: B's neighbours are A and C.

feedback.correct: $(2 + 4)/2 = 3$: the mean of A and C.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Average the values at B's neighbours.

byKey.self: You averaged B's own 0 in as well: $(2 + 0 + 4)/3 = 2$. Without a self-loop B is left out.
byKey.sum: You added A and C. The step divides by B's degree, 2.

explain.text: B's neighbours A and C hold 2 and 4, so B gets 3. A walker at B moves to A or C with chance $\tfrac12$ each, and the expected value there is 3.

screens.title: How far k steps reach
screens.prose: Now every node has a self-loop, so a step averages a node with its neighbours: $\tilde{\mathbf D}^{-1}\tilde{\mathbf A}$. Node S starts with 1 and every other node with 0.
screens.question: Tap every node that holds a value above 0 after two steps.

hints.text: After one step S, a and f hold something.
The second step passes it one more link: b and d. S keeps a share through its self-loop.

feedback.correct: S, a, f, b and d: every node within two links of S.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Each step moves the value one link further, and the self-loops keep what is already there.

byKey.one: That is one step. The second step carries it from a to b and d.
byKey.all: c and e are three links from S, so two steps do not reach them.

explain.text: One step reaches S's neighbours, two steps their neighbours. With self-loops nothing already reached drops back to 0, so after $k$ steps the value covers every node within $k$ links.

screens.title: Values against probability
screens.prose: In `markov` l14 a walker moves probability: the row of chances times $\mathbf P$, so the mass moves by $\mathbf P^\top$ as a column. Averaging values uses $\mathbf P$ itself. The two are different steps on the same graph.
screens.question: The walker starts at D. After one step, what is the chance that it is at A?

hints.text: From D the walker must take D's only link.
The value step gave A $\tfrac13$, but that was a mean, not a chance.

feedback.correct: 1: D's only link leads to A.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Follow the walker from D for one step.

byKey.values: That is the averaged value at A, $(\mathbf P\mathbf x)_A$. The walker's chance moves by $\mathbf P^\top$, so all of D's mass goes to A.

explain.text: The walker's probability moves along links and keeps its total of 1, so all of it lands on A. Averaging takes each node's mean of its neighbours instead, so A gets only $\tfrac13$. One sums over where mass comes from; the other averages over where the walker goes.

screens.title: Two numbers a node
screens.prose: Each venue now holds two numbers, a spread and a volume: A $(2, 10)$, B $(0, 4)$, C $(4, 6)$, D $(6, 8)$. Stack them as the rows of $\mathbf X$ and take $\mathbf P\mathbf X$.
screens.question: What is the second number in venue A's row of $\mathbf P\mathbf X$?

hints.text: Each column is averaged on its own.
Volume at B, C and D: $(4 + 6 + 8)/3$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Average the second column over A's neighbours.

byKey.own: You averaged A's own 10 in as well: $28/4 = 7$.
byKey.first: That is the first number, the averaged spread. The question asks for the volume.

explain.text: $\mathbf P\mathbf X$ averages each column the same way, so A's row is $(\tfrac{10}{3}, 6)$. Features as vectors change nothing: every coordinate gets the same weights.

screens.title: Arrows have a direction
screens.prose: Banks lend to banks. Write $A_{ij} = 1$ when bank $i$ has lent to bank $j$: arrows B to A, C to A and A to D. The values are A 5, B 1, C 3 and D 9.
screens.question: What does A collect in one step of $\mathbf A\mathbf x$?

hints.text: Row A of $\mathbf A$ has a 1 in each column $j$ with $A_{Aj} = 1$.
A has lent to D only.

feedback.correct: 9: row A has its only 1 at D, the bank A lent to.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read row A of $\mathbf A$.

byKey.incoming: You followed the arrows into A, from B and C. That is row A of $\mathbf A^\top$; $\mathbf A\mathbf x$ reads row A of $\mathbf A$.
byKey.both: You used the arrows both ways. A directed $\mathbf A$ is not symmetric, so only the arrow out of A counts.

explain.text: $(\mathbf A\mathbf x)_i$ sums over the $j$ with $A_{ij} = 1$, so A collects D's 9: a lender reads the banks it is exposed to. Collecting along arrows into a node is $\mathbf A^\top\mathbf x$; choose the direction on purpose.

screens.title: A square that never settles
screens.prose: Four venues form a square, the edge case of `markov` l14. A starts with 1. Slide through the plain averaging steps, with no self-loops.
screens.question: Without self-loops, what does A hold after 100 steps?

hints.text: The values swap between two patterns.
On even steps A and C hold $\tfrac12$; on odd steps B and D do.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac12$: 100 is even, and A holds $\tfrac12$ on every even step.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the pattern in the first four steps.

byKey.settle: You expected the values to settle at $\tfrac14$. Without self-loops they swap sides for ever.
byKey.odd: That is A on an odd step. 100 is even.

explain.text: The square splits into two sides, A and C against B and D, and every link crosses. Plain averaging swaps the sides each step, so A holds $\tfrac12$ on even steps for ever. With self-loops the values settle at $\tfrac14$.

canvas.caption: With self-loops, step 6: close to 0.25 everywhere.

screens.title: Where averaging settles
screens.prose:
Repeated multiplication keeps the eigenvalue-1 part (`eigen` l4). For $\mathbf P$ that part is $\mathbf 1\boldsymbol\pi^\top$, so on a connected graph that does not split into two sides,

$$\mathbf P^k\mathbf x \to (\boldsymbol\pi^\top\mathbf x)\,\mathbf 1, \qquad \pi_i = \frac{d_i}{2|E|}.$$
screens.question: With the values A 2, B 0, C 4 and D 6, what does every venue settle on? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: $\boldsymbol\pi = (\tfrac38, \tfrac28, \tfrac28, \tfrac18)$.
$\tfrac38 \cdot 2 + \tfrac28 \cdot 0 + \tfrac28 \cdot 4 + \tfrac18 \cdot 6$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Weight each value by the venue's share $\pi_i$.

byKey.mean: You took the plain mean, 3. Busy venues weigh more: each value counts by its degree.

explain.text: The settled value is the walk's long-run average of $\mathbf x$, $\boldsymbol\pi^\top\mathbf x = 2.5$. A venue with more links is visited more, so its value counts more.

screens.title: Message passing in code
screens.prose: Write `message_step(A, X, self_loops)`: add the identity when `self_loops` is true, divide each row of the matrix by its sum, and multiply by `X`, a vector or one row a node. Then write `k_steps(A, X, k)`: $k$ plain steps, with no self-loops.
screens.question: Write `message_step` and `k_steps`.

mutants.symptom: Divides by column sums, which on a directed graph or for a node's value mixes the wrong degrees.
Uses $\mathbf P^\top$, moving mass as the walk does instead of averaging values.
Ignores self_loops, so a node never keeps a share of its own value.
Symmetrises the directed graph, so a bank also reads the banks that lent to it.

hints.text: `P = A / A.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)`, then `P @ X`.
`k_steps` calls `message_step(A, X, False)` $k$ times.

feedback.correct: Your steps average along rows of $\mathbf A$, keep a share with self-loops, and repeat exactly $k$ times.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Divide each row by its own sum and multiply $\mathbf P\mathbf x$: B should get 3.
byKey.test-2: With self-loops add $\mathbf I$ before dividing: B should get $(2 + 0 + 4)/3 = 2$.
byKey.test-4: Three plain steps from 1 at D give $(\tfrac29, \tfrac1{12}, \tfrac1{12}, 0)$.
byKey.test-6: On a directed graph row $i$ of $\mathbf A$ lists the arrows out of $i$: average along them, without transposing or symmetrising.

explain.text: A step is $\mathbf D^{-1}\mathbf A\mathbf X$, or $\tilde{\mathbf D}^{-1}\tilde{\mathbf A}\mathbf X$ with self-loops. Repeating it is $\mathbf P^k\mathbf X$.

screens.title: Does it settle?
screens.prose: Write `settles(A, x, k, tol)`: run $k$ plain steps of $\mathbf D^{-1}\mathbf A$ on `x` and return `True` when the last step changed every value by less than `tol`. A self-loop is a 1 on the diagonal of `A`, so the same function covers both kinds of step.
screens.question: Write `settles`.

widget.how: Submit runs 9 hidden tests: the venues, the square without and with self-loops, a run too short to settle, and two nodes that swap. Then two more runs on the venues, and a pair that swaps by 0.002 beside 20 settled nodes. Last, the venues at 22 steps, the first step that moves every value by less than 0.001. Each must return True or False exactly.

mutants.symptom: Compares the end with the start, not with the step before.
Takes two steps at a time, so the square's swap looks settled.
Adds self-loops, so the square settles when it should not.
Uses the mean change, which can be small while one node still moves.
Runs one step too few, so the check looks at the 21st step, which still moves a value by more than 0.001.

mutants.source:
import numpy as np


def settles(A, x, k, tol):
    A = np.asarray(A, dtype=float)
    P = A / A.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    for _ in range(10000):
        new = P @ x
        if np.max(np.abs(new - x)) < tol:
            return True
        x = new
    return False
mutants.symptom: Ignores $k$ and runs until the change is small, so a run too short to settle looks settled.

hints.text: Keep the vector from before the last step.
`np.max(np.abs(x - prev)) < tol`.

feedback.correct: Your check settles the venues and the looped square, and catches the plain square's swap.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Compare the last step with the one before it, not with the start: the venues end far from 1 at D but stop changing.
byKey.test-2: The plain square must not settle: take one step at a time, and add no self-loops of your own. It swaps sides every step.
byKey.test-8: Check the largest change, not the average: two nodes still swap by 0.002 while 20 others sit still.
byKey.test-4: Three steps from 1 at D still move values by more than 0.001.
byKey.test-9: Run exactly $k$ steps: the 22nd is the first to move every value by less than 0.001.

explain.text: The square swaps between two patterns, so its last step never shrinks. A self-loop on the diagonal breaks the swap, and the values settle at $\tfrac14$.

screens.title: Stress in a funding network
screens.prose: A central bank H funds four banks, which deal only with H. A shock hits L1 with stress 1. Each day every bank's stress becomes the mean over itself and its counterparties, $\tilde{\mathbf D}^{-1}\tilde{\mathbf A}$.
screens.question: What stress does L2 carry after two days? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: After one day H holds $\tfrac15$: it averages itself and its four banks.
On day two L2 averages itself, 0, and H, $\tfrac15$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Day one reaches H; day two reaches the other banks.

byKey.one-day: That is H after one day. L2 averages its own 0 with that on day two.
byKey.no-loop: You dropped the self-loops: L2 would copy H's $\tfrac14$. The banks average over themselves too.

explain.text: Day one carries the stress to H, $\tfrac15$. Day two carries half of that to each other bank, 0.1. In $k$ days the stress reaches banks up to $k$ links away, smaller at each step.

ideas: A message-passing step replaces each node's value by a combination of its neighbours' values; with $\mathbf P = \mathbf D^{-1}\mathbf A$ it is the expected value where the walker lands next.
$k$ steps reach nodes up to $k$ links away, and every coordinate of a vector feature is averaged with the same weights.
On a connected graph that does not split into two sides, $\mathbf P^k\mathbf x$ settles at $\boldsymbol\pi^\top\mathbf x$ everywhere; on two sides it swaps for ever unless self-loops are added.

formula.name: One step and its limit
formula.tex: \mathbf x \to \mathbf D^{-1}\mathbf A\,\mathbf x, \qquad \mathbf P^k\mathbf x \to (\boldsymbol\pi^\top\mathbf x)\,\mathbf 1
formula.note: The walk moves probability by $\mathbf P^\top$; averaging uses $\mathbf P$.

summary.trap: On a directed graph, mixing up $\mathbf A\mathbf x$ (row $i$: the arrows out of $i$) with $\mathbf A^\top\mathbf x$ (the arrows into $i$).

quiz.prose: A path links node 1 to node 2 and node 2 to node 3. They hold 3, 0 and 6.
quiz.question: After one plain step of $\mathbf D^{-1}\mathbf A$, what does node 2 hold? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Average node 2's two neighbours.

byKey.self: You included node 2's own 0. A plain step has no self-loop.

explain.text: Node 2's neighbours hold 3 and 6, so it gets 4.5.

quiz.prose: Plain averaging, $\mathbf x \to \mathbf D^{-1}\mathbf A\mathbf x$, runs for many steps on a connected graph.
quiz.question: On which graph can the values keep swapping for ever?

options.text: One whose nodes split into two sides with every link between the sides
One that contains a triangle of three linked nodes
options.why: A triangle gives an odd cycle, which ends the swapping: the walk can return in 3 steps as well as 2.

options.text: One with a hub linked to many others
options.why: A hub alone does not cause swapping. The cause is two sides with every link across.

options.text: Any graph, unless every node has the same degree
options.why: Equal degrees are not needed: the four venues have degrees 3, 2, 2, 1 and still settle.

feedback.correct: Two sides with every link across: the values swap sides each step.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think of the square.

explain.text: On such a graph each step moves every value to the other side, so the pattern repeats every 2 steps. A self-loop, or any odd cycle, stops it.

quiz.prose: A hub H is linked to three leaves. H holds 4 and the leaves hold 0. Plain averaging runs with self-loops added to every node.
quiz.question: What value does every node settle on? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Weight each value by its node's degree with the loop, over the total.

byKey.mean: You took the plain mean, 1. The hub counts by its degree.
byKey.noloop: You used the degrees without loops, 3 out of 6. With loops the hub has 4 of the 10.

explain.text: With loops the degrees are 4, 2, 2, 2, total 10, so the hub's share is $\tfrac{4}{10}$ and every node settles at 1.6.
